phase1.intro:
Overriding is different from the overloading you've already seen.

Want to start with what overriding actually is, or the polymorphism it unlocks?

dialogue: A subclass takes a method it inherited and [[key:replaces the whole implementation with its own version, same name, same parameters]]. Dog's `makeSound()` has the exact same signature as Animal's, but a completely different body — that's [[term:overriding]].

The `@Override` annotation isn't required by the compiler, but [[key:it's a safety net worth always using]] — misspell the method name and `@Override` flags it immediately instead of quietly compiling a brand new unrelated method.

stickyNote.flavor: 🔄 same name, same params, new body
stickyNote.definition: A subclass replaces a parent method's implementation, keeping the same name and parameters. @Override catches signature mistakes at compile time.

topics.buttonText: What happens when an Animal variable actually holds a Dog?
dialogue: `Animal myDog = new Dog();` stores a Dog inside an Animal-typed variable, and calling `myDog.makeSound()` still runs Dog's version, not Animal's.

[[term:Runtime polymorphism]] means [[key:Java decides which version of an overridden method to run based on the object's ACTUAL type, not the type of the variable holding it]] — decided while the program runs, not at compile time.

stickyNote.flavor: 🎭 the object's real type wins, not the variable's
stickyNote.definition: When calling an overridden method, Java runs the version matching the object's actual type — decided at runtime, not compile time.

topics.buttonText: Can I override a static method?
dialogue: [[warn:You cannot override a static method]]. Static methods belong to the class itself, not to any particular object, so there's no "actual object type" for Java to check at runtime in the first place.

stickyNote.flavor: 🚫 no object, no runtime type to check
stickyNote.definition: Static methods belong to the class, not an object, so there's no object type at runtime for Java to dispatch on — they can't be overridden.

phase1.openingDialogue: Overriding replaces an inherited method entirely — and it's what makes runtime polymorphism possible. 🎭

phase2.errorMessage:
Dog.java:8: error: method does not override or implement a method from a supertype
    @Override
    ^
1 error

(And if you remove @Override, it compiles but doesn't override! The parent method is still called.)
phase2.explanation:
[[warn:makesSound isn't the same method as makeSound]] — one extra letter, and Java sees two completely unrelated methods instead of an override. `@Override` is exactly what catches this: it tells the compiler "I claim this overrides something from my parent," and the compiler checks that claim against Animal and finds nothing matching.

[[key:If @Override weren't there at all, this mistake would compile silently]] — Dog would just end up with an extra method nobody calls, and `dog.makeSound()` would keep quietly running Animal's original version instead of the one you meant to write. That's exactly why `@Override` is worth using every single time you intend to override something — it turns a silent logic bug into a loud compile-time error.

phase3.openingDialogue: Time to override! Give methods a new twist~ 🔄

mcq.question:
What determines which overridden method actually runs when you call myAnimal.makeSound()?

A) The declared type of the variable (Animal)
B) The actual runtime type of the object it refers to (e.g. Dog)
C) Whichever version was compiled first
D) It's random

phase4.selfChallenge:
Create a class Shape with method area() that returns 0.0.
Create Rectangle and Circle subclasses that override area():
• Rectangle: area = width * height
• Circle: area = Math.PI * radius * radius

In main, create Shape references to Rectangle and Circle and print their areas.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: @Override wasn't always part of Java — annotations in general (including @Override) were only added in Java 5, back in 2004. Before that, a misspelled override was a purely silent bug with zero compiler help, which is part of why this exact mistake used to be so much more common in real production code.
phase5.openingDialogue: One more thing before you swap out more behavior~
